## Intersection Rigidity in Closed Symplectic Manifolds

A fundamental theme in symplectic topology concerns the extent to which subsets of a symplectic manifold resist displacement under the action of symplectomorphisms. This paper establishes that such resistance is not a monolithic phenomenon but rather organizes itself into a **hierarchy of intersection rigidity properties**. Within this hierarchy, different classes of sets exhibit varying degrees of robustness: some subsets can be displaced by suitably chosen symplectomorphisms, while others remain stubbornly non-displaceable, intersecting their image under *any* symplectomorphism isotopic to the identity (or, in stronger cases, under any symplectomorphism whatsoever). Distinguishing these levels of rigidity, and identifying precisely which geometric or dynamical data force a set into the more rigid strata, is one of the central goals of this work.

### New Examples: Moment Map Fibers

A key contribution is the identification of previously unrecognized instances of intersection rigidity. Specifically, we show that certain **fibers of moment maps associated to Hamiltonian torus actions** possess strong rigidity properties. These fibers, which need not correspond to the most commonly studied cases (such as fixed points or the fiber over the barycenter of the moment polytope), are shown to be non-displaceable via arguments that exploit the interplay between the torus action, the underlying Floer-theoretic invariants, and the combinatorial structure of the moment polytope. This extends the known landscape of rigid subsets well beyond the classical examples arising from toric geometry and monotone fibers of the moment map.

### Monotone Lagrangian Submanifolds

Building on the foundational work of P. Albers and of P. Biran–O. Cornea, we demonstrate that **monotone Lagrangian submanifolds** also fit naturally into this hierarchy of intersection rigidity. Albers' work on the relationship between displaceability and the vanishing of certain Floer-theoretic pairings, together with the Lagrangian quantum homology and cluster complex machinery developed by Biran and Cornea, provided the first substantial evidence that monotone Lagrangians carry robust rigidity properties. Our results extend and reinforce this picture, showing that monotone Lagrangian submanifolds occupy a definite, identifiable place within the broader rigidity hierarchy, with their non-displaceability properties following from the same unifying framework that governs the moment map fibers and singular sets discussed below.

### Rigidity of Singular Sets via Poisson-Commutative Subalgebras

Beyond smooth submanifolds, the hierarchy extends to certain **possibly singular sets** that arise naturally from the algebraic structure of the Poisson bracket. Given a Poisson-commutative subalgebra of the smooth functions on the symplectic manifold, one can associate to it distinguished level sets — often singular, in contrast to the smooth fibers of a completely integrable system — that inherit rigidity properties from the algebraic and dynamical structure of the subalgebra. We show that such sets, despite the potential presence of singularities, still exhibit non-displaceability phenomena analogous to those enjoyed by smooth fibers of moment maps. This significantly broadens the class of examples to which intersection rigidity techniques apply, moving beyond the traditionally smooth setting of Lagrangian submanifolds and toric fibers.

### Obstructions to Semi-Simplicity of Quantum Homology

The methods developed to establish these rigidity results simultaneously yield structural information about **quantum homology**. In particular, we uncover **geometric obstructions to the semi-simplicity of the quantum homology algebra** of the ambient symplectic manifold. These obstructions manifest through the existence of the rigid sets described above: their non-displaceability is incompatible with a fully semi-simple quantum homology, thereby linking an algebraic property of the quantum homology ring to concrete geometric configurations in the manifold. The proofs of these obstruction results rely crucially on **Floer-theoretic partial symplectic quasi-states** — functionals on the space of smooth functions, constructed via spectral invariants and Floer homology, that generalize the symplectic quasi-states of Entov and Polterovich to the partial (non-semi-simple) setting. These quasi-states serve as the technical bridge connecting the dynamical non-displaceability statements to the algebraic structure of quantum homology, and their construction and analysis form a central technical pillar of the paper.

### Summary

Taken together, these results paint a unified picture: intersection rigidity is a graded phenomenon admitting a rich hierarchy, populated by moment map fibers, monotone Lagrangians, and singular level sets of Poisson-commutative subalgebras alike, all governed by a common Floer-theoretic mechanism. This mechanism, realized through partial symplectic quasi-states, not only produces new rigidity phenomena but also reveals deep structural constraints on the quantum homology of the ambient symplectic manifold, in particular obstructing its semi-simplicity in the presence of sufficiently rigid geometric configurations.

# Introduction

The study of rigidity phenomena in symplectic topology has long centered on the tension between the flexibility permitted by volume-preserving transformations and the surprising constraints imposed by the symplectic form itself. A fundamental manifestation of this tension is the question of which subsets of a closed symplectic manifold $(M, \omega)$ can be displaced from themselves by a Hamiltonian or symplectic diffeomorphism, and which subsets are forced—by purely topological or algebraic reasons rooted in Floer theory—to intersect their images under any such map. This paper contributes to this circle of ideas by establishing a refined hierarchy of intersection rigidity properties, and by producing new, previously unrecognized instances of rigid sets across several natural geometric contexts.

Our approach relies on the machinery of partial symplectic quasi-states, as developed by Entov and Polterovich building on ideas from Floer theory and quantum homology. A partial symplectic quasi-state is a functional on (a subset of) smooth functions on $M$ satisfying quasi-linearity, monotonicity, and a Poisson-commutativity condition, and its existence is intimately tied to the structure of the quantum homology ring of $M$—in particular, to the presence of idempotents and the associated splitting of quantum homology into fields. Sets that are "heavy" or "superheavy" with respect to such quasi-states inherit strong non-displaceability properties: heavy sets cannot be displaced from certain other heavy sets, while superheavy sets cannot be displaced from any set that is merely non-trivial in an appropriate sense, and moreover cannot be displaced by symplectomorphisms preserving the relevant quasi-state. This dichotomy between heaviness and superheaviness already suggests a hierarchy of rigidity, and one of the central aims of this paper is to sharpen, extend, and organize this hierarchy, situating known examples within a broader taxonomy and producing further intermediate and extremal cases.

We apply this framework to three distinct classes of sets that arise naturally in symplectic geometry. First, we consider fibers of moment maps associated to Hamiltonian torus actions, and identify a spectrum of behaviors depending on the position of the fiber relative to the momentum polytope and its combinatorics: some fibers are shown to be superheavy, others merely heavy, and yet others fail to satisfy any rigidity property recognizable through this machinery, illustrating how the quasi-state formalism can distinguish fine gradations of rigidity even within a single toric or almost-toric fibration. Second, we turn to monotone Lagrangian submanifolds, whose Floer-theoretic invariants—namely their Floer homology with bulk deformations and the associated eigenvalues of quantum multiplication by the first Chern class—determine whether they support a well-defined partial quasi-state and, consequently, whether they exhibit heaviness or superheaviness. This yields new examples of non-displaceable monotone Lagrangians, including cases not previously accessible by classical Floer-theoretic non-displaceability criteria. Third, we study sets defined via Poisson-commutative subalgebras of smooth functions, such as level sets of integrable systems and Gelfand-Cetlin-type constructions, showing that the existence of a sufficiently rich commutative family gives rise to quasi-states detecting heaviness of associated level sets, thereby generalizing the moment map picture to a broader class of integrable and near-integrable systems.

Beyond the intrinsic interest of these new rigidity examples, our results have structural consequences for the algebraic side of the theory. The existence of partial symplectic quasi-states associated to superheavy sets is obstructed by, and in turn obstructs, the semi-simplicity of the quantum homology ring: a fully semi-simple quantum homology admits an idempotent decomposition compatible with quasi-state constructions in a way that can preclude certain configurations of heavy or superheavy sets from coexisting, while conversely the discovery of specific rigid sets can be used to detect non-semi-simplicity or to constrain the possible idempotent structure. We exploit this interplay to derive new geometric obstructions to semi-simplicity, translating Floer-theoretic rigidity phenomena—expressed through the existence and properties of quasi-states associated to our examples—into concrete restrictions on the ring-theoretic structure of quantum homology.

Taken together, these results deepen the dictionary between Floer-theoretic algebraic structures and geometric rigidity phenomena, extend the catalogue of known non-displaceable and partially rigid sets in symplectic manifolds, and demonstrate that the hierarchy of heaviness and superheaviness is considerably richer and more sensitive to geometric data—such as moment map combinatorics, monotonicity and Floer-theoretic invariants of Lagrangians, and the structure of Poisson-commutative subalgebras—than previously appreciated. We view this work as a step toward a more complete understanding of the layered structure of symplectic rigidity and its algebraic underpinnings in quantum homology.

# Hamiltonian and Lagrangian Mechanics: Foundations of Classical Physics

Classical mechanics underwent a profound transformation in the 18th and 19th centuries through the development of two powerful mathematical frameworks: Lagrangian and Hamiltonian mechanics. These formulations extended Newton's laws of motion into more abstract and versatile systems of analysis.

## The Lagrangian Formulation

Joseph-Louis Lagrange developed his approach to mechanics in the late 18th century, introducing what is now known as the Lagrangian function, typically denoted as L. This function is defined as the difference between kinetic energy (T) and potential energy (V) of a system:

L = T - V

The power of the Lagrangian approach lies in its use of generalized coordinates, which allows physicists to describe complex systems—including those with constraints—without needing to work directly with forces. Instead, the equations of motion are derived from the principle of least action, which states that a physical system evolves along the path that minimizes (or extremizes) the action integral.

The Euler-Lagrange equations, derived from this principle, provide a systematic method for obtaining equations of motion for virtually any mechanical system, from simple pendulums to complex multi-body systems.

## The Hamiltonian Formulation

Building upon Lagrange's work, William Rowan Hamilton introduced an alternative formulation in the 1830s. The Hamiltonian, denoted H, is obtained through a Legendre transformation of the Lagrangian and typically represents the total energy of a system, expressed in terms of position and momentum coordinates rather than position and velocity.

Hamilton's equations offer several advantages:
- They provide a symmetric treatment of position and momentum
- They form the foundation for Hamiltonian mechanics' extension into statistical mechanics
- They serve as a crucial bridge to quantum mechanics through canonical quantization
- They reveal deep connections to symplectic geometry

## Contributions from Albers

Various researchers named Albers have contributed to different scientific fields, though it's worth noting that the name "Albers" is perhaps most famously associated with Heinrich C. Albers, known for the Albers projection in cartography—a conic map projection that preserves area. While this represents a different domain from classical mechanics, it illustrates how mathematical frameworks developed for one purpose (in this case, geometric transformations) often find surprising applications across scientific disciplines.

In mathematical physics more broadly, various scholars have worked on extending Hamiltonian and Lagrangian methods to new contexts, including field theory, general relativity, and quantum systems. These extensions demonstrate the remarkable versatility of the theoretical framework established by Lagrange and Hamilton, which continues to influence how physicists approach problems ranging from celestial mechanics to particle physics.

## Conclusion

The Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formulations represent more than mathematical reformulations of Newtonian mechanics—they embody deeper physical principles about symmetry, conservation laws (as formalized in Noether's theorem), and the underlying structure of physical theories. Their continued relevance in modern physics, from classical mechanics to quantum field theory, testifies to the profound insight of their original creators.

# Abstract

We investigate a hierarchy of intersection rigidity properties for compact subsets of closed symplectic manifolds, building on the theory of partial symplectic quasi-states introduced by Entov and Polterovich. A subset is called *symplectically rigid* if it cannot be displaced from itself, or more generally from certain related sets, by Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms; various strengthenings of this notion — including superheaviness, stability, and the property of being a "non-displaceable in a strong sense" — yield a natural stratification of subsets according to the robustness of their intersection properties with Hamiltonian images of other sets.

In this paper we systematically compare these rigidity notions, clarifying their logical relationships and showing that, in general, the hierarchy is strict: we construct explicit examples of subsets that are heavy but not superheavy, superheavy but not stable, and so forth, using probes coming from partial symplectic quasi-states associated to spectral invariants and quantum homology idempotents. Our main tools include the calculus of quasi-states, the theory of spectral invariants for Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms, and Poisson bracket invariants, which allow us to detect fine intersection properties beyond mere non-displaceability.

As applications, we establish new instances of Hamiltonian non-displaceability for singular fibers of moment maps and for other naturally occurring subsets in toric and non-toric symplectic manifolds, and we produce examples distinguishing the various rigidity classes in symplectic manifolds such as products of spheres and toric varieties equipped with non-trivial quasi-states. Our results shed light on the subtle interplay between quantum homology, Poisson geometry, and the C⁰-symplectic topology of subsets, and suggest further refinements of the rigidity hierarchy in higher-dimensional and non-monotone settings.

# Displacement Rigidity in Symplectic Manifolds: A Summary

## Background

A central theme in symplectic topology concerns **displaceability**: given a subset $A$ of a symplectic manifold $(M,\omega)$, does there exist a symplectomorphism (or Hamiltonian diffeomorphism) $\phi$ such that $\phi(A) \cap A = \emptyset$? Non-displaceable sets are considered "symplectically rigid" and often serve as obstructions detected by Floer-theoretic invariants.

## Main Result

Research in this area (building on work of Entov–Polterovich, Fukaya–Oh–Ohta–Ono, and others) establishes a **hierarchy of rigidity** among fibers of moment maps for Hamiltonian torus actions, and more generally among monotone Lagrangian submanifolds:

- **Toric moment map fibers.** For a toric symplectic manifold with moment map $\mu: M \to \mathfrak{t}^*$, generic fibers (Lagrangian torus orbits) are displaceable, but *special* fibers — particularly those satisfying a monotonicity or "balanced" condition — are **non-displaceable**. This non-displaceability is detected via Floer cohomology: a fiber $L = \mu^{-1}(u)$ is non-displaceable whenever its Lagrangian Floer cohomology $HF(L,L;\Lambda)$ (with appropriate bulk deformations or quantum parameters) is nonzero.

- **Monotone Lagrangians and quasi-morphisms.** Using quasi-states and quasi-morphisms constructed from spectral invariants (Entov–Polterovich), one shows that **monotone Lagrangians** — those satisfying $\omega|_{\pi_2(M,L)} = \lambda \, \mu_{Maslov}|_{\pi_2(M,L)}$ for $\lambda>0$ — often sit at "heavy" or "superheavy" points of the moment polytope, forcing non-displaceability even when naive volume or homological arguments are inconclusive.

- **Comparative rigidity.** Crucially, the result shows this rigidity is **not uniform**: some non-displaceable fibers are more robust than others, distinguished by:
  - Whether they remain non-displaceable under **all** Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms versus only symplectomorphisms isotopic to the identity;
  - Whether their Floer cohomology remains nonzero after **bulk deformation** by ambient cohomology classes;
  - Stability under **partial (relative) quasi-morphisms**, showing some fibers "shadow" quasi-states from open subsets of the polytope while others require deformation by all of $H^*(M)$.

## Key Techniques

1. **Floer-theoretic invariants**: Non-vanishing of $HF(L,L)$, computed via the Fukaya–Oh–Ohta–Ono potential function, gives the primary obstruction.
2. **Bulk deformations**: Twisting Floer differentials by classes in $H^{even}(M;\Lambda)$ reveals fibers whose non-displaceability depends on ambient geometry, not just the Lagrangian itself.
3. **Spectral quasi-morphisms**: Entov–Polterovich theory produces symplectic quasi-states $\zeta$ satisfying $\zeta(L) \neq 0 \Rightarrow L$ superheavy $\Rightarrow$ non-displaceable, giving a finer invariant than Floer cohomology alone.
4. **Explicit examples**: In toric manifolds like $\mathbb{CP}^2$ blown up at points, or Fano toric varieties, moment polytopes contain distinguished points (e.g., the barycenter for the monotone case) where the fiber is non-displaceable, contrasted with nearby fibers that are displaceable — showing rigidity is a **codimension phenomenon** within the polytope, not generic.

## Conclusion

The result demonstrates that displaceability is a subtle, non-monotonic invariant: **being "special" (monotone, or corresponding to interior/singular points of the moment polytope) confers extra rigidity**, and different non-displaceable Lagrangians can be ranked by *how* they resist displacement (Floer-theoretic vs. quasi-morphism vs. bulk-deformed), giving a refined landscape of symplectic rigidity beyond a binary displaceable/non-displaceable dichotomy.

# Abstract

We investigate rigidity phenomena for Lagrangian intersections through the lens of Floer-theoretic invariants, with particular attention to obstructions arising from the semi-simplicity of quantum homology. Building on the structural theory of quantum homology algebras, we establish new intersection results for Lagrangian submanifolds under hypotheses formulated in terms of idempotent decompositions and spectral invariants associated to Floer cohomology.

Our approach proceeds by analyzing the behavior of Floer homology under deformation of almost complex structures and Hamiltonian isotopies, exploiting the algebraic structure imposed when the quantum homology of the ambient symplectic manifold splits as a direct sum of fields. In this semi-simple setting, we show that idempotents give rise to a decomposition of Lagrangian Floer theory into distinguished summands, each supporting nontrivial spectral invariants that persist under perturbation. This yields sharp lower bounds on the number of intersection points between a fixed Lagrangian and its Hamiltonian images, extending and unifying several known rigidity statements including generalizations of the Arnold conjecture in this framework.

We further examine cases where semi-simplicity fails, showing how the presence of nilpotent elements or non-split quantum homology algebras leads to genuinely different rigidity behavior, and we construct examples illustrating the necessity of our hypotheses. A central technical tool is a refined study of the Piunikhin-Salamon-Schwartz isomorphism and its compatibility with the ring structure on quantum homology, which allows us to transport information between the Floer-theoretic and quantum categories. As applications, we obtain new non-displaceability results for monotone Lagrangian tori and toric fibers, recovering previously known constraints while producing sharper bounds in several families of examples, and we discuss connections to the study of quasi-morphisms and quasi-states on symplectic manifolds arising from spectral invariants.

Our results highlight the interplay between the algebraic structure of quantum homology and the geometric rigidity of Lagrangian submanifolds, and suggest further directions for understanding intersection phenomena in symplectic manifolds whose quantum homology exhibits partial or no semi-simplicity.

# Hierarchies of Lagrangian Non-Displaceability via Quantum Homology and Pearl Complexes

## Abstract

We investigate a stratified framework of non-displaceability phenomena for Lagrangian submanifolds arising from the algebraic structure of quantum homology, with particular emphasis on the interplay between Floer-theoretic obstructions and the semi-simplicity of the quantum homology ring. Building on the foundational approach of Biran and Cornea, who introduced the pearl complex as a Morse-theoretic model for Lagrangian quantum homology and established a spectral sequence linking classical Morse theory to Floer-theoretic invariants, we develop a hierarchy of non-displaceability criteria organized according to the depth of algebraic structure required to detect obstruction. At the coarsest level, this hierarchy recovers classical non-displaceability results detectable purely through quantum homology being nonzero as a module; intermediate levels invoke the ring structure and the existence of idempotents, following the framework in which Biran-Cornea's iterated cone decompositions yield obstructions to displacing entire Lagrangian skeleta and their intersections. At the finest level, we incorporate the results of Albers relating Floer homology of Lagrangian intersections to Morse-theoretic spectral invariants via the PSS-type isomorphisms, thereby refining the hierarchy to detect non-displaceability at the level of individual Floer trajectories and their persistence under Hamiltonian perturbation. Central to our analysis is the semi-simplicity of the quantum homology ring $QH_*(M)$: when $QH_*(M)$ decomposes as a direct sum of fields via a complete set of orthogonal idempotents, each idempotent summand localizes distinct symplectic invariants and gives rise to a corresponding family of Lagrangian submanifolds that are mutually non-displaceable, generalizing the Entov-Polterovich construction of quasi-states and superheavy sets. We show that this semi-simple decomposition induces a refinement of the Biran-Cornea cone-decomposition hierarchy, wherein each stratum corresponds to a spectral idempotent and the associated non-displaceability results interpolate between the module-level and trajectory-level statements of Albers. As an application, we exhibit new families of non-displaceable Lagrangian tori and toric fibers in symplectic manifolds with semi-simple quantum homology, and we discuss the extent to which the hierarchy stabilizes under symplectic reduction and blow-up, situating our results within the broader program of detecting rigidity phenomena through the algebraic topology of the Fukaya category.

---

**Keywords:** Lagrangian non-displaceability, quantum homology, semi-simplicity, pearl complex, Floer homology, symplectic topology, Biran-Cornea cone decomposition, spectral invariants
